opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's funny, because in many ways it feels like déjà vu. When I started graduate school in the 1980s, working with Douglas Hofstadter, the big debate was between what people called symbolic AI, the "good old-fashioned AI" of logic, rules, and explicit knowledge representation, and the connectionists, who were just having a resurgence with the parallel distributed processing work and backpropagation. The rhetoric then was remarkably similar to what you hear now. One side said intelligence is fundamentally about manipulating symbols and you can't get reasoning or compositionality out of statistical association. The other side said symbols are brittle and hand-engineered, and real intelligence has to emerge from learning over distributed representations.

What's different now is the scale, and the fact that the learning side has had enormous practical success. Large language models do things that I think very few people, including me, would have predicted even ten years ago. So the debate has shifted from "can neural networks do anything interesting?" to "what exactly are these systems doing, and is it the kind of thing that will generalize the way human understanding does?"

But I actually think the framing of "symbolic versus learning" was never quite right, then or now. What we were trying to do with Copycat was neither pure symbolic AI nor pure connectionism. We were interested in things like analogy, concepts that are fluid and context-sensitive, the interplay between perception and abstraction. Those questions are still the hard ones. Humans clearly learn, but we also form abstractions we can reason with and transfer to new situations very flexibly, often from just a few examples. Current systems are impressive, but they still struggle with that kind of robust abstraction and analogy, especially when you move them away from the distribution of their training data.

So I'd say the core questions haven't really been resolved. What's changed is that we have much more powerful tools to probe them, and the stakes are higher because these systems are being deployed everywhere. And I'd hope that this time around the field can be a bit less tribal about it, and focus more on careful evaluation of what these systems actually understand, rather than just declaring victory for one camp or the other.

r001.rationale: The response calls the debate “déjà vu” and says its rhetoric was remarkably similar to today’s, describing the same symbolic AI versus learning divide.

r002.rationale: It contrasts explicit symbolic knowledge with learned distributed representations, but does not identify the question of what to build in versus learn end to end as a recurrence of an innateness-versus-learning debate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because in some ways it feels like déjà vu. When I started graduate school at Michigan in the mid-1980s, working with Douglas Hofstadter, the field was really split. You had the symbolic camp, the expert systems people, who believed intelligence was fundamentally about manipulating symbols according to rules, and that if you could just write down enough knowledge in the right formal language, you'd get there. And then you had the connectionists, who were just coming back into prominence with backpropagation, saying no, intelligence emerges from lots of simple units interacting, and you don't program it, you learn it.

And what Doug and I were doing with Copycat sat somewhat uncomfortably in between. We had symbolic structures, concepts, but they were fluid, they had activations that spread and decayed, and the whole system was built around parallel stochastic processes rather than a deductive engine. So I was always a bit skeptical of both camps' purity claims.

What's different now is that the learning side has won so decisively in terms of practical results. Nobody in the 1980s could have imagined something like a large language model producing fluent text about almost anything. So the debate has shifted. It's no longer "can learning systems do anything interesting?" It's "do these systems actually have the kind of robust, compositional, abstract understanding that the symbolic people were always insisting on?" And I think the honest answer is that we don't know, and the evidence is mixed. They do surprisingly well on many things and then fail in ways that reveal they're not forming the concepts we assume they are.

So the old questions haven't gone away. They've just been reframed. People are asking whether abstraction and compositionality can emerge purely from scale and data, or whether you need something built in, some inductive bias toward structure. That's really the same argument Fodor and Pylyshyn were having with the connectionists in 1988. The vocabulary has changed, the systems are enormously more capable, but the core puzzle of how you get genuine understanding, concepts that can be flexibly recombined and applied to novel situations, is still very much open. I find that both humbling and encouraging. It means the questions were the right questions all along.

r001.rationale: The response says the current debate is a reframing of the old questions and calls the dispute over abstraction and compositionality “the same argument” from the 1980s.

r002.rationale: It contrasts learning abstraction from scale and data with building in an inductive bias toward structure, then identifies this as the earlier connectionist debate.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a lot that feels familiar. When I was starting out, there was this debate between symbolic AI, where you explicitly represent concepts and rules, and neural networks, where you learn from examples. And often those were presented as competing explanations of intelligence, rather than approaches that might each capture something important.

Today the learning systems are much more powerful, and that changes the substance of the debate. We can ask questions experimentally that we couldn’t really ask then. But the underlying questions are remarkably similar: What needs to be built in? What can be learned? How do you get from recognizing patterns to understanding concepts and applying them in new situations?

I’ve always been interested in that connection. I think human intelligence involves both learning from experience and being able to work with fairly abstract concepts. The difficult part is explaining how those concepts arise and how they stay connected to the situations we encounter. Just saying “we need symbols” or “we need learning” doesn’t really answer that. That’s where I think the most interesting work still is.

r001.rationale: The response says the earlier symbolic AI versus neural network debate and today’s debate share “remarkably similar” underlying questions, clearly characterizing them as substantially the same.

r002.rationale: It contrasts what needs to be built in with what can be learned, and presents those as recurring underlying questions from the debate she encountered when starting out.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, there’s a lot that feels familiar. When I was starting out, there was already this debate about whether intelligence comes from explicitly represented symbols and rules, or whether it can emerge from learning in networks of relatively simple units. The balance of enthusiasm has shifted dramatically, but many of the underlying questions are still with us.

I think one problem is that we often treat “symbolic” and “learning” as opposite ends of a single axis. But you can ask how a system learns and, separately, what kinds of representations it learns. Could a neural network develop representations that support abstraction and the flexible use of concepts? Could a system with symbolic representations learn those representations instead of having people supply them? Those are much more interesting questions to me than which camp is going to win.

My own interests have been in analogy and abstraction: how we recognize the same underlying idea in situations that look very different. Learning is clearly essential to that, but just saying that a system learns doesn’t tell us how it forms concepts or when it will be able to apply them appropriately. So the successes today are very exciting, but I think some of the old questions have become more urgent rather than going away.

r001.rationale: The response says the debate feels familiar and describes the earlier dispute between explicit symbols and rules and intelligence emerging through learning, adding that many underlying questions remain.

r002.rationale: It asks whether symbolic representations should be supplied by people or learned by the system, directly expressing the recurring question of what to build in versus learn.
